task_name: The groom, as an act of the app

rubric.result: The objective promises two things. (a) 'runs the plugin's program over the epic's spec': groom-epic.ts:331-336 calls this.groom.run({ root, spec: before.spec!, repository, milestone: before.milestone! }) with the spec and milestone the read gave, and then re-reads so the answer is what the milestone really holds (line 338-340). (b) 'is refused without running it while the spec is not frozen or its committed copy is not published': GroomEpic.REFUSED holds NO_SPEC, DRAFT and AWAITING_PUBLICATION and the early return at line 327-329 happens before any call to the port, so a refused groom never reaches EpicGroom.run — the acceptance criterion this task serves. Both halves are in the diff; nothing the objective promises is missing.

The TDD line names it('a spec that is not frozen refuses the groom and the program is never run') and fixes the assertion as 'the result's state is draft and the EpicGroom double's run was not called'. The test body asserts exactly that: expect(groomed.state).toBe(EpicGroomState.DRAFT) and expect(flow.groom.runAsked).toEqual([]), over a read that answers Mother.draftRead(). Its named boundary pair is also there: 'a groomable epic runs the groom once and answers the issues the milestone holds afterwards' asserts runAsked equals a single call carrying Mother.frozenSpec(), Mother.REPOSITORY and Mother.MILESTONE — the spec, repository and milestone the read gave — and groomed.issues equals issuesAfter, which is the second read's list while the first read's was [], so it does discriminate second from first. Same assertion, same input, same expected value as the plan wrote it.

The Contract block declares three symbols and the diff states them name by name. GroomEpicParams: constructor({ root, repository }: { root: CheckoutRoot, repository: RepositoryName }) — identical, same names and order. EpicGroomed: readonly state: EpicGroomStateValue, milestone: string | null, plan: GroomPlan | null, issues: readonly EpicIssue[] — all four, same types, same order. GroomEpic: static readonly REFUSED: readonly EpicGroomStateValue[], constructor({ read, groom }: { read: ReadEpicGroom, groom: EpicGroom }), async execute(params: GroomEpicParams): Promise<EpicGroomed> — identical. The prose of the task is honoured too: REFUSED holds exactly the three rungs before the groom (no-spec, draft, awaiting-publication, checked against the six members of EpicGroomState in read-epic-groom.ts), the refused branch returns that rung so the boundary can name it, and the plan of the FIRST read travels in the result (line 340 passes plan: before.plan while state, milestone and issues come from 'after'). No Current state or Call site block accompanied this task and none is owed: the route that presses this arrives in a later task. No error, no constant and no exported name differs from the brief.

Rows the diff bears on: D-13 (no phase is stored) — the action derives everything by asking ReadEpicGroom twice and stores nothing, which is the row implemented with its value. D-11 (a yardstick is imported from the plugin, never reimplemented) — the action grows no second opinion about whether a spec is frozen or published; it reads the state off EpicGroomRead and delegates the groom to the EpicGroom port. D-23 (the groom waits for the merge of the spec's publication) — AWAITING_PUBLICATION is in REFUSED, so the groom stays refused until the committed copy is readable on the default branch. D-10 (everything new under backend/ is TypeScript) — both new files are .ts with erasable syntax only, and npm run typecheck is green. D-7 (no write to a pull request) — nothing here writes to one. D-6/D-22 (the gates are acts of the app, pressed only from the page) — the gate key lives at the route, which this task does not touch, and nothing in the diff opens a path around it. Rows the diff leaves alone (D-1, D-18, D-21, D-25, D-14 and the block of the other decisions) comply by not being touched. No row is reopened.

Exemplars: backend/src/application/actions/freeze-spec.ts is the action that refuses before mutating, and groom-epic.ts plays the same role with the same idiom — a Params class and a result class frozen at construction and declared beside the use case, dependencies by name through the constructor, no suffix on the type, no try/catch turning errors into the invoker's vocabulary. backend/__tests__/application/freeze-spec.test.ts and read-epic-groom.test.ts are the test exemplars, and the new test matches them line for line in shape: doubles extending the real port/use-case classes, a Mother of named scenarios (draftRead, awaitingPublicationRead, noSpecRead, groomableRead, groomedRead), a Flow holding the doubles with a static named constructor (Flow.readingOnce) and a run() that builds the use case from it.

Rules read for this diff: conventions/architecture.md — the file sits in application/actions/, the folder is the discriminator and there is no suffix; the use case depends on ReadEpicGroom and the EpicGroom port and never on an adapter; it declares its result object (EpicGroomed) rather than returning a raw map, as 'The shape of a use case' requires. conventions/style.md — no comment, no docstring, every function hangs off a type, all identifiers English. conventions/domain.md — value objects frozen at construction; no tool's noun enters (EpicGroom, EpicGroomed, GroomPlan are domain words, not 'gh' or 'node'). conventions/simplicity.md — nothing added beyond the contract, and the non-null assertions on before.spec and before.milestone are the simplicity-conforming choice here: a throw at those lines would be 'an unreachable check is not a check', since read-epic-groom.ts guarantees both are set once the three refused rungs are past; the same idiom is already in the host (read-epic-groom.ts:88, spec.title()!). conventions/decisions.md — the partition {no-spec, draft, awaiting-publication} is declared exactly once in the tree (grep over the repo: only groom-epic.ts:42-44 names it as a set), so the rule about a partition of a closed vocabulary declared in more than one place is not tripped. conventions/boundaries.md has no subject: this is the application layer, nothing here talks to an external system or projects outwards. conventions/testing.md — the assertions are on the observable effect (what the port received, what the use case returned), the doubles raise when nobody wrote an answer for a request (ReadEpicGroomDouble throws on an unanswered nth ask), values are real instances, and the arrange is not built with the piece under test. Note, not a finding: testing.md's table says 'every port, doubled by construction' and here the doubled collaborator is a use case (ReadEpicGroom) rather than a port — that is the constructor the plan's Contract block prescribes verbatim, so the implementer could not have written it otherwise, and answering the query twice by order is the only way to express 'the issues are the second read's, not the first's'.

conventions/defects.md, rule by rule. Closed vocabulary: complies — the classification travels as EpicGroomStateValue, the closed vocabulary of read-epic-groom.ts, never as a loose string or a boolean; there is no dispatch with a catch-all branch, only a membership test against the frozen REFUSED list, and the refused rung itself is returned so the consumer can tell the three apart. Raw map as the return value of logic: complies — the use case returns EpicGroomed, a declared result object; the object literal at line 331-336 is a parameter typed by the EpicGroom port's own Grooming type, not a return value, and it is the host idiom (freeze-spec.ts does the same with branch.commit). Two fields that have to agree: complies — the absence is in the type (milestone: string | null, plan: GroomPlan | null), there is no flag repeating what another field says and no sentinel: no empty string for 'no milestone' and no zero for 'never groomed'. An error named for where it happens: no subject — the diff declares and raises no error; the only throw is inside the test double and it names what happened ('was asked a Nth time with no answer written for it').

Delivery shape: no document of either yardstick prescribes a delivery pattern for a new use case with no caller yet, and the change is purely additive — two new files, no signature altered, no call site left on an old path.

Does not apply: the diff has no '-' lines at all. Both files are new (203 + 73 insertions, 0 deletions), so there is no pre-existing assertion, case or test that could have been removed, relaxed or rewritten. I also checked that the neighbouring suite was left alone — read-epic-groom.test.ts and freeze-spec.test.ts are not among the touched paths.

The promised behaviour is produced by production code. The refusal lives at groom-epic.ts:327-329 (the early return before this.groom.run) and the re-read at line 338-340, both in src/application/actions/. The test's scaffolding (Mother, Flow, ReadEpicGroomDouble, EpicGroomDouble) only supplies inputs and records what the port received; no expected value is hard-coded where a production line should be. The discriminating case: in 'a groomable epic runs the groom once...' the first read answers GROOMABLE with issues [] and the second answers GROOMED with issuesAfter, so expect(groomed.issues).toEqual(issuesAfter) can only pass because line 340 reads after.issues rather than before.issues — the assertion is on a production decision, not on the double's setup. Likewise expect(flow.groom.runAsked).toEqual([]) in the three refusal tests fails the moment the early return is removed.

The diff writes exactly the two files **Files:** declares, both marked (create) and both genuinely new, and nothing inside them exceeds the task. Every production symbol is one the Contract block names; there is no extra helper, no rename, no refactor of a neighbouring module and no adjacent fix. The six tests in the file are exactly the six **Tests:** lists, in name and in number — no seventh was added and none was dropped. Nothing named in ### Out of scope is touched: ct-groom.mjs, groom.js, slices.js and gh-issue-map.js are untouched, there is no --reconcile, no --project, no Project v2, no merge and no write to a pull request, no dispatcher change and nothing about choosing the next slice. There is no hunk of the plan file in this diff, so no amendment was written and none needed ruling: the task's **Files:**, **Tests:**, **TDD:** and **Verification:** are the ones the plan was committed with.

Six new tests, all in backend/__tests__/application/groom-epic.test.ts, and the three properties hold for each. Deterministic: no clock, no Date.now, no network, no filesystem, no randomness and no sleep — the only date is the literal '2026-09-14' inside Mother.frozenSpec()'s text, and the whole flow is in-memory doubles. Isolated: every test builds its own Flow with its own doubles inside the test body; the shared statics on Mother are frozen value objects (GroomPlan, GroomPlanIssue, EpicSpec, CheckoutRoot all Object.freeze themselves at construction) and the mutable recorders (asked, runAsked) live on per-test double instances, so nothing leaks between tests and no test depends on the order of the file, on a port, a fixed path or a directory. Verifies real behaviour: the assertions are on what the use case returned (groomed.state, groomed.issues, groomed.plan) and on what the port received (flow.groom.runAsked), never on a mock's call count standing in for an effect nor on a constant the test just defined; with the production lines reverted none of them would pass. I loaded control-tower-loop:test-driven-development to measure the finer half and found nothing in it or in its testing-anti-patterns reference that these tests contradict and that the plan did not itself dictate: its 'Minimal — "and" in the name? Split it' row would touch names like 'a spec that is not frozen refuses the groom and the program is never run', but that name is written literally in the task's **TDD:** and **Tests:** lines, and ct's own conventions/testing.md ('its name is the sentence, and it says what is guaranteed and why') takes precedence and endorses it — one behaviour, the refusal, stated with its consequence. No finding.
